clue.text: Skill collecting articles deep down

indicators.note: something collecting other items holds them within itself, so the skill word surrounds the articles

parts.note: art is skill, as in the art of conversation
THE and A are the definite and indefinite articles

explanation.surface: A talent that gathers up assorted objects, buried somewhere deep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collecting' puts THE and A, the two English articles, inside ART after its first letter: A-THEA-RT.
explanation.definitionFit: At heart is an idiom meaning in one's true nature, beneath the surface, the same as deep down.

clue.text: Round a lake, relaid paths with this, perhaps

definitions.text: Round a lake, relaid paths with this, perhaps

indicators.note: the shuffled path letters go round the other letters, enclosing them
relaid means laid out again, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is the usual abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: Paths circling a lake have been resurfaced, possibly using this material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relaid' rearranges PATHS to ASPHT, and 'Round' puts A and L inside it after the H.
explanation.definitionFit: Asphalt is the tarry surfacing material commonly used to resurface roads and footpaths.

clue.text: Strike illegally, putting crown jewels in danger?

definitions.meaning: in boxing, hitting below the belt is a foul blow
crown jewels is a jokey term for a man's genitals, which sit below the belt

explanation.surface: A dirty blow that endangers the royal regalia.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means landing a foul punch beneath the waistline, and figuratively acting unfairly.

clue.text: A great deal required for such a call at whist

definitions.meaning: a large quantity, a great deal
in solo whist, ... is a bid to win nine or more tricks

explanation.surface: Many tricks are needed to make a particular bid in a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue links the two senses: a large haul of tricks is what this bid demands.
explanation.definitionFit: Abundance means plenty; in solo whist it also names a bid to take at least nine tricks.

clue.text: Speed in system, post-mortem reveals

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits within the following words
reveals says the words disclose an answer concealed among their letters

explanation.surface: An autopsy shows how fast something moved through the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is the speed or pace of music or of an activity.

clue.text: Training scheme daughter studied

parts.note: PE is physical education, training of the body at school
a ruse is a crafty scheme or trick
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter in family trees

explanation.surface: A daughter studied the outline of a training programme.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse something is to read or examine it carefully, so perused is a synonym of studied.

clue.text: Lawman's family enthralled by member of the clergy

indicators.note: being enthralled by someone is being held captive by them, so the family word is held inside

parts.note: a parson is a parish priest
kin means one's family or relatives

explanation.surface: A policeman's relatives are captivated by a vicar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lawman' suggests a sheriff, but it is the man behind Parkinson's Law.
explanation.definitionFit: C. Northcote Parkinson coined Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time available, making him a lawman.

clue.text: Anger involving female's firearm

indicators.note: involving means enclosing, so the anger word wraps round the letter for female

parts.note: to rile someone is to anger them

explanation.surface: An angry woman reaches for her gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a long-barrelled gun, one type of firearm.

clue.text: Careful to include king, his consort, and friend to argue with?

indicators.note: the careful word is made to include the king letter, holding it inside

parts.note: sparing means careful or economical with something
R is the abbreviation for king, from Latin rex
a consort is a spouse or partner

explanation.surface: A frugal monarch's household budget covers the king and his queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to include' puts R inside SPARING. The definition is playful: a boxer's practice opponent, or anyone you enjoy debating.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparring partner is a training opponent in boxing, figuratively someone you regularly argue with in friendly fashion.

clue.text: Side with boy, oddly, and step out of line

indicators.note: oddly means strangely, so these letters are arranged in a strange new way

explanation.surface: Taking a boy's side unexpectedly means breaking the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' looks like a call for odd letters, but it rearranges SIDE and BOY.
explanation.definitionFit: To disobey is to break rules or orders, an idiom for stepping out of line.

clue.text: Novel published, another by female convicts

parts.note: a book that is published is put out by its publisher
more means an additional one, another
lag is British slang for a convict, especially an old lag

explanation.surface: A novel is released, followed by a second one written by women prisoners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective, but it is the definition. Lag is British slang for a long-serving prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Put Out More Flags is a 1942 novel by Evelyn Waugh, a title example of the class novel.

clue.text: A principal's further on

parts.note: the principal of a school is its head

explanation.surface: A school principal has moved further forward in the career.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahead means in front or in advance, so further on in position or progress.

clue.text: Colour of a lovebird, variegated

indicators.note: variegated means patchily mixed in colour, so the letters of these words are mixed up too

explanation.surface: Describing the plumage of a small parrot whose feathers come in several colours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variegated' rearranges the letters of A LOVEBIRD.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive drab is a dull greenish-brown shade, famous from military uniforms, so it is a colour.

clue.text: Made a record of what was said in seized messages

definitions.text: Made a record of what was said

parts.note: took means grabbed, seized
notes are short written messages

explanation.surface: A spy logs intercepted communications that had been confiscated.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking notes is writing down a record of spoken content, such as a lecture or meeting.

clue.text: Fine leg spinner, balding

parts.note: fine means thin, as in a fine thread
in cricket, the leg side of the field is also called the on side
a top is a toy that spins

explanation.surface: A cricket report praising a fine leg-spin bowler whose hair is going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine leg' and 'leg spinner' are both cricket terms (a fielding position and a type of bowler); here the words split differently.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin on top is a common idiom for losing hair from the crown, that is, balding.

clue.text: Character in Grease from outskirts of Sydney?

parts.note: the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters, here the edges of the city name joined by the ampersand

explanation.surface: Asking whether a figure from the musical Grease hailed from the suburbs of Sydney.
explanation.walkthrough: The edge letters of Sydney are S and Y: writing that phrase out gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandy Olsson is the heroine of the musical and film Grease, played on screen by Olivia Newton-John.

clue.text: Sight in glasses slightly reduced

indicators.note: slightly reduced means losing just a little, so one letter comes off the end

parts.note: spectacles are glasses for the eyes

explanation.surface: Someone's vision is a little worse while wearing glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slightly reduced' drops the final S of SPECTACLES.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is an impressive sight or display, such as a grand public show.

clue.text: Joint initially twisted in marshy area

indicators.note: the letter is placed in the marsh word, inside it

parts.note: a mire is a stretch of swampy, boggy ground

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone twisted a knee or ankle joint while stuck in a bog.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitre is a woodworking joint where two pieces meet at an angle, as at a picture-frame corner.

clue.text: Mummy's boy's exploits before work

indicators.note: before places the exploits word ahead of the work word

parts.note: to milk something is to exploit it fully
OP is short for opus, Latin for a work

explanation.surface: A mother's son has adventures before getting a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exploits' looks like a noun (deeds) but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A milksop is a feeble, timid man, much like the insult mummy's boy.

clue.text: Landlord's private stock included

indicators.note: the stock word is included within the private word, sitting inside it

parts.note: inner means private, as in one's inner thoughts
to stock goods is to keep them for sale

explanation.surface: A landlord keeps a personal supply of something stashed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stock' looks like a noun (goods) but works as the verb, to keep goods for sale; 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An innkeeper runs a pub or inn; in Britain a pub's manager is commonly called the landlord.

clue.text: Former British soldier, or cadet in need of training

indicators.note: something in need of training must be reshaped, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Describing an old soldier or a young cadet who still has to be drilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Redcoat was the nickname for British army soldiers of the past, from their scarlet tunics.

clue.text: Feudal superior's story — good part recalled by child, finally

parts.note: a story can be a lie, as in telling stories

indicators.note: recalled is read as called back, so this word runs back to front

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A medieval lord's tale includes a good part remembered by a child at last.
explanation.definitionFit: In the feudal system a liege lord was the overlord to whom vassals owed allegiance and service.

clue.text: Number in Dorset he rang?

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits within the following words

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a man phoned a particular telephone number in Dorset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a figure, but it means something that numbs. Dorset is an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was an early anaesthetic, a substance that numbs, so a number in the crossword sense.

clue.text: Become dejected when inferior diamonds shown up

indicators.note: in a down clue, shown up means written upwards, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: poor means of low quality, inferior
D is the abbreviation for diamonds in card games

explanation.surface: A card player becomes downcast when weak diamonds are exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shown up' reads POOR D upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To droop is to sag or lose spirit, so to become dejected.

clue.text: Weary and drawn? That's about right

indicators.note: about means around, so the drawn word goes round the letter for right

parts.note: a drawn match is tied, ending level

explanation.surface: Someone looks exhausted and haggard, and agrees that is a fair description.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawn' looks like a second meaning of weary, but it is the sporting sense, a tied game.
explanation.definitionFit: Tired and weary are straightforward synonyms describing fatigue after effort.

clue.text: Help me out, now it's your turn!

definitions.text: Help me out, now it's your turn!

parts.words: Help me out, now it's your turn!
parts.note: the whole clue is a plea for someone else to do what they can, a common request for assistance

explanation.surface: Someone asks a friend for assistance, handing over the task.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an everyday request asking another person to try their best to help or sort a problem.

clue.text: A supporter of mine?

parts.note: reads like a fan of the speaker, but mine is a coal mine and the supporter holds up its roof

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a person is one of their fans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of mine' looks possessive; it means of a mine, a colliery.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit prop is a timber or steel post holding up the roof of a mine shaft or tunnel.

clue.text: Clown and I make a mistake on board vessel

indicators.note: on board a vessel means within it, so these letters sit inside the vessel word

parts.note: a pot is a vessel for holding liquid or food
to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: A clown confesses to blundering while aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship, but it is a cooking pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierrot is the sad white-faced clown character from French pantomime and commedia dell'arte.
